In the I90 (Π) spectrum, several Rydberg peaks converging to the 4Σ− (D) and 2Σ− (D) core-ionized states, Rydberg (Q) and Rydberg (D), are resolved. Considering that the exchange splitting in the Rydberg series is nearly the same as in the core-ionized states of 4Σ− and 2Σ− (1.1 eV) and the intensity ratio of the Rydberg (Q) to Rydberg (D) states is almost 2:1, peaks observed in the I90 spectrum are assigned mainly to npπ (Q) and n'pπ (D) Rydberg states. In the following discussion on the Rydberg–valence mixing in the σ channel, we start from the diabatic representation, such as σ* (D), σ* (Q), 3s(D), 3s(Q), 3p(D), and 3p(Q), where σ*, 3s, and 3p are 2pσ* valence, 3sσ Ry, and 3pσ Rydberg electrons.

1. Lower σ* Region

The symmetry-resolved ion-yield spectrum I0 in Fig. 14 clearly exhibits that the two main features B and C have σ symmetry. These intensities should come from the valence σ* component, irrespective of complicated Rydberg-valence mixing. We could simply assign feature B to σ* (D) and feature C to σ* (Q), considering that the transition probability of 1s→σ* (Q) is twice as large as that of 1s→σ* (D). One of the most puzzling spectral characteristics in the energy region in question is the lower-energy part 539 eV observed in the experiment: a very long energy tail and a sharp first peak followed by some smaller peaks [23, 26, 33, 34, 91, 102, 104–116]. The accepted interpretation of this feature is that the main intensity arises from the dissociative σ* (D) resonance, which is lower than σ* (Q) due to exchange interaction of the σ* electron [23, 83]. On the other hand, the fine features 539 eV were interpreted as a weak vibrational progression in the bound 3s(Q) state embedded in the σ* (D) manifold [23] and a Fano profile due to weak interaction between the bound and continuum-like state [26]. The interaction between the 3s(Q) and σ* (D) states could be small, because they have different ion cores Q and D and 3s and 2pσ* have different orbital characters [26]. However, σ* (D) can be mixed with σ* (Q) [83, 102, 108], and the small σ* (Q) component would contribute to interaction with 3s(Q). On the other hand, the strong Rydberg–valence mixing between 2pσ* (Q) and 3pσ (Q) is found in the higher energy part 542 eV [26, 34, 91, 105], as shown in Fig. 15.

The theoretical spectra produced by the coupled wave-packet propagation in the diabatic states [108] are shown in Fig. 16 in comparison with the experimental Σ spectra. In Fig. 16, the partial contributions of the Q and D channels are shown by ignoring the weak coupling between them. The overall spectral shapes of both partial cross-sections have roughly Gaussian shapes owing to absorption to the dissociative states σ* (Q) and σ* (D). The Gaussian shapes are split and the intensity is reduced near the crossing points between the dissociative σ* states and the bound Rydberg states, because the latter transition dipoles are smaller compared to the former state. Note that the structures below the potential crossing point exhibit a smooth continuum (dissociative) shape, while the structures above the crossing point have a vibrational character shaped by the interfering coupled wave packets simultaneously evolving in the core-excited states. The largest splits in the middle of the spectral packets of both Q and D channels near 540 eV are caused by mixing with the 3p(Q) and 3p(D) Rydberg states, respectively, whose interactions with the dissociative states are largest (Fig. 17). The low-energy tail <539 eV of the total spectrum has a continuum profile resulting from both dissociative σ* (D) and σ* (Q) states. We would like to pay attention to the spectral profile of the D channel where the vibrational structure is almost invisible (Fig. 16). It is a weak vibrational progression on the top of the D spectrum in the regions 539–540 and 541–543 eV.

The formation of the first resonance-like feature in the theoretical spectrum can be better understood with the help of Fig. 17 [108]. When the X-ray energy increases from the region below the crossing S, the overlap between the ground-state wave function and the continuum wave functions grows, because the classical turning point in the dissociative state moves to shorter bond lengths, closer to the equilibrium geometry. Near the crossing point S, the transition dipole abruptly falls, due to the increased 3s(Q) component, and causes a dip in the absorption spectrum. Thus, the initial increase of the cross-section is followed by a sudden decrease, after which the cross-section grows again. The broad tail to the lower energy is mostly due to the σ* (D) state of dissociative character. The intensity for the excitation to the dissociative state or repulsive state σ* (Q) is now reduced 540 eV due to the intensity transfer from the σ* (Q) to the 3p(Q) state near the crossing point S1 (Fig. 17). When tuning the photon energy at feature B, the 1s→σ* (D) state is possibly dissociated to the atomic O 1s→2p 3P excited state with no curve crossing, as shown in Fig. 15, resulting in atomic Auger decay [103, 114, 115].

2. Higher σ* Region

In contrast to the mixing related to the D channel, the higher and stronger 1s→σ* (Q) state can interact with several Rydberg states with the same ion core Q, especially, npσ (Q) series with the same orbital character. In the I0 spectrum, the npσ (Q) Rydberg and n'pσ (D) series show single peaks similarly to the npπ (Q) and n'pπ (D) Rydberg series, except that the 3pσ (Q) Rydberg transition cannot be assigned to a single peak. The potential energy curves shown in Fig. 15 [26] indicate that the 1s→σ* (Q) repulsive state can strongly interact with the 1s→3pσ (Q) Rydberg state in the FC region. Then, a bound state (upper state) is produced through the avoided curve crossing between σ* (Q) and 3pσ (Q) and several vibrational excitations become allowed. Thus, the 3pσ (Q) Rydberg state is strongly perturbed by the repulsive σ* (Q) state with the same ion core, and has an unusual vibrational enhancement as clearly observed in the I0 spectrum in Fig. 14.

A similar Rydberg–valence mixing is more or less expected in other npσ Rydberg states; in fact, the npσ (Q) Rydberg series is much stronger than the n'pσ (D) Rydberg series. Due to strong Rydberg–valence mixings through the avoided curve crossings in the Q channel, the repulsive 1s→σ* (Q) excited state cannot be isolated from the Rydberg states. The 1s→σ* (Q) excitation disperses its intensity mainly to the 1s→npσ (Q) Rydberg series, which has bound-state character, and reduces dissociative character. Therefore, the molecular Auger decay is observed when tuning the photon energy at feature C.

VI. ARPIS of SO2

A. Core–Valence Exchange versus Spin–Orbit Interactions

The spin–orbit (SO) splitting of the core electrons is directly observed in XPS. Even in the 2p photoabsorption spectra, the 2p SO splitting of third-row and heavier elements is large and is easily distinguishable. The singlet and triplet 2p excited states are strongly and indistinguishably mixed with each other through SO or jj coupling. However, in the second-row elements, such as phosphorus and sulfur, the 2p SO is not satisfactorily analyzed due to a comparable intraatomic core–valence EX splitting. Spin–Orbit is still a major factor in the core-to-Rydberg excited state with a small ST (EX) splitting, but is only one of some important factors in the core-to-valence excited state with a relatively large ST (EX) splitting [116–120], as also discussed in O2 in comparison with S2 and Se2. In recent high-resolution photoelectron spectroscopy, it is possible to reveal another small splitting in the 2p3/2 manifold due to the molecular field (MF) effect [121–124].

The 2p excitation spectra of molecules containing second-row elements, such as sulfur and phosphorus, are thought to be generally characterized by the presence of two closely related manifolds of the SO pair, 2p3/2 (lower in energy, twice as strong) and 2p1/2. The SO interaction is inherently of atomic core character. Spectral assignments in the 2p excitation spectra are often based on identification of corresponding lines in the 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 manifolds, which are clearly resolved in recent high-resolution 2p photoelectron spectra, together with a very small splitting in the 2p3/2 manifold due to the MF splitting [121–124]. However, in some excited states of the P 2p and S 2p excitation spectra of PF3, SF6, OPF3, SPF3, NSF3 and other related systems, it is found to be too difficult to assign the 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 SO pair [116–120]. In the 2p excitation, the excited electron contributes to the core–valence EX and is coupled with a singlet or triplet spin in excitation from the closed-shell ground state, whereas in the 2p ionization there is not a corresponding EX interaction. When the ST (EX) splitting (ΔST) is much larger than the SO splitting, the ST mixing through SO is negligible and no SO pair is observed, as precisely discussed for P 2p excitation of PF3 [118]. The 2p excitation spectra of third-row and heavier elements are much simpler, because the deeper core increases the SO interaction and weakens the core–valence EX interaction. In this sense, both EX and SO are exclusively important in the 2p excitation of the second-row elements by chance.

Exchange involving the 2p core electron is anisotropic, depending on the relation between the 2p orbital direction and molecular structure. In some sulfur containing molecules, it is experimentally revealed that the S 2p and excited electrons have EX compatible to the 2p SO interaction for parallel 2pπ→π* transitions and EX smaller than SO for perpendicular 2pσ→π* transitions. In other words, the jj coupling scheme is not applicable to the parallel transitions. Thus, we can expect the following general scheme for anisotropic EX interaction versus 2p SO interaction:

1. Perpendicular transition (I90): EX < SO

The jj coupling scheme is valid.

Singlet (bright) components distributed equally to lower and higher states.

2. Parallel transition (I0): EX > SO

The jj coupling scheme is broken (intermediate coupling).

Excitation energy is blue shifted due to large EX.

Lower states have more triplet (dark) components.

Higher states have more singlet (bright) components.

B. jj-Coupling versus Intermediate Coupling

The S 1s ARPIS spectra of a C symmetry planar molecule, SO2, have shown three valence states below the Rydberg manifold, 3b1 (π*), 9a1, and 4b2 [125]. Figure 18 shows S 2p ARPIS of the S 2p→3b1 (π*) region [84]. Although high-resolution photoabsorption spectra in this region have been analyzed [126] by referring to an already-reported theoretical analysis [127] based on nonrelativistic HF solutions combined with an empirical SO splitting parameter, detailed SO and EX characteristics have not yet been discussed. The S 2p →3b1π* excited states have the 1,3B1, 1,3A2, and 1,3A1 symmetries using the 2p orbitals of a1, b2, and b1 symmetries. From the X1 A1 ground state the singlet 1A2 excited state is electric dipole forbidden. The 1A1←X1A1 and 1B1←X1A1 excitations are dipole allowed, being transitions parallel and perpendicular to the polarization vector of photons, respectively. Even after taking into account the SO interaction, the singlet 1B1, 1A2, and 1A1 excited states are not mixed with one another, but each singlet state is mixed with two dipole-forbidden triplet states of 3B1, 3A2, and 3A1 through SO, resulting in three electronic states for each singlet symmetry.

In Fig. 18, the MF, EX, and SO interactions are taken into account step by step in comparison with the S 2p ARPIS of SO2. First, the small MF splitting in the 2p ionization is shown without either SO or EX. Second, considering the excited electron in 3b1π* explicitly, the EX(+MF) splitting at the zero SO limit is shown. As expected, the ST (EX) splitting in the parallel 2pb1→3b1π*(1,3A1) transition is much larger than ST in the perpendicular transitions, 2pa1→3b1π*(1,3B1) and 2pb2→3b1π*(1,3A2). In Fig. 18, the SO interaction is finally taken into account in addition to MF and EX [124]. The 1A1 manifold indicates a rather large ST splitting 0.9 eV; therefore, the lowest of the three SO states in the parallel excitation hardly borrows intensity from the dipole-allowed 1A1 component and is almost invisible. In the 1A1 manifold observed in the parallel polarization I0, the peak intensity in the 2p1/2 region is comparable to (a little larger than) that in the 2p3/2 region, in good agreement with the theoretical prediction. On the other hand, in the 1B1 manifold observed in the perpendicular polarization I90, the ST (EX) splitting is small, 0.1 eV, and SO is the most significant. Then, the jj coupling scheme predicts that the 2p3/2 (L) region is much stronger than the 2p1/2 (H) region, though the intensity ratio I(H)/I(L) is not 0.5 (at the zero EX limit), but 0.65. In this case, even the lowest state in the 2p3/2 region can get intensity from the 1B1 component and is observable.

VII. Some Extensions Related to ARPIS Technique

The angular anisotropy in the emission direction of photoproducts formed following inner-shell excitation and ionization can be applied to various kinds of investigation in molecular inner-shell photoprocesses. Since Siegel and co-workers [128] reported on their hypothetical experiment for the angular distributions of photoelectrons from fixed-in-space molecules in 1976, experimentalists started to think of how to realize this situation. In 1992, Zähringer et al. [129] performed theoretical calculations for angle-resolved Auger rates from spatially oriented molecules, where the authors suggested that the full angular distribution of Auger electrons is measurable by coincidence detection between the momenta of the Auger electron and atomic ion that is produced by the prompt dissociation following the molecular Auger decay. The first experimental realization of this kind was reported as the angular distribution measurements of photoelectrons from fixed-in-space molecules, which was achieved by introducing the coincidence detection between the photoelectron and fragment ion [130]. After this pioneering work, many investigations for the molecular frame photoelectron angular distribution (MFPAD), which are essentially based on the same concept as [130], have been carried out intensively [131–157]. Since the applications of the angular anisotropy in the dissociation process following the inner-shell photoexcitation, some recent investigations other than MFPAD are summarized in the following Section VII.

A. Auger Electron Emission from Spatially Fixed Molecules

It is quite natural to extend the experimental technique for measuring MFPAD to the Auger electron emission. The most detailed information on the MOs involved in the process is obtainable by measuring the angular distributions of Auger electrons from fixed-in-space molecules. As demonstrated in this chapter, thanks to the rapid progress of the experimental techniques associated with synchrotron radiation, vibrational spectroscopy in the inner-shell excitation region of low-Z molecules has become feasible. The findings through the studies on the resonant Auger processes and their theoretical analyses impel us to give up the traditional idea that the molecular dissociation begins with the Auger final state when the Auger transition is terminated [158]. This means that the Auger decay cannot be treated separately from the primary photoexcitation process. However, it is widely believed that the decay process following inner-shell ionization, namely, the normal Auger decay, can be interpreted as a two-step process in which the Auger decay is treated independently of the initial ionization process. The experiment to show the limitation of this picture has been performed on CO after C1s ionization [159]. The de-excitation of the C (1s)−1 core–hole state predominantly populates the three lowest singlet states X1Σ(5σ−2), A1Π(5σ−11π−1), B1Σ(5σ−14σ−1) of the doubly ionized CO molecule.

The angular distributions after both σ and π ionization for the unresolved X and A states are shown in Fig. 19, in comparison to those for the B state: the angular distribution patterns for the X and A states are almost isotropic, but those for the B state are very rich in structure and remarkably different from each other. The latter observation completely differs from both regular Auger electron angular distributions from randomly oriented molecules, and the theoretical prediction for the fixed-in-space angular distributions of Auger electrons by Kuznetsov and Cherepkov [160], where the angular distribution patterns after both σ and π ionization should be the same. Sundin et al. [161] have demonstrated with vibrational resolution that the PCI effect distorts the line shapes of both the photoelectron and Auger decay spectra recorded at the C1s shape resonance position. The results for the B state in Fig. 19 may imply that the PCI effect affects the Auger electron not only in its energy distribution, but also in its angular distribution. In order to examine such new findings in more details, Guillemin et al. [159] performed the similar experiments at various photon energies. It was found that the angular patterns for the X and A states exhibit no photon energy dependences, while there is a dramatic photon energy dependence of the angular distribution patterns for the B state in each ionization channel. They concluded that their observation can be a direct evidence for a dynamical angular correlation between the Auger electron, the residual ion, and the photoelectron. The authors believed these results to be evidence for the breakdown of the two-step model for the molecular Auger decay and merit further theoretical investigation.

Weber et al. [162] later performed a similar experiment using a different experimental setup based on the imaging detection, named COLTRIMS (Cold Target Recoil Ion Momentum Spectroscopy [163]), which led to controversial results for the dependence of the angular distributions of Auger electrons on the photoionization channels and the photon energy. Since then, several groups have studied the Auger electron angular distributions in the molecular frame for different systems [164–170]. In order to gain complete information on the photoionization and Auger decay processes, a new experimental setup toward an extended analysis of the Auger-electron–photoelectron angular correlation and emission of Auger electrons and photoelectrons from fixed-in-space molecules seems to be ready to operate [171]. The controversy in the angular distributions for the Auger electrons following the C 1s photoionization of fixed-in-space CO molecules [159, 162] will be solved in the near future.

B. Metastable Fragment Detection

As demonstrated in Section III–VI, definite assignments for the discrete resonances have been given by the combined utilization of the high-resolution ARPIS method with sophisticated theoretical calculations. The performance of the ARPIS method is, however, limited by the inherent background owing to the 1s ionization continuum, which tends to hide weaker multiexcitation structures. In particular, the large cross-section of the shape resonance severely prevents one from identifying multiexcitation structures associated with the parallel transition. The background contribution from the 1s ionization continuum can be reduced by measuring partial electron yields. Neeb et al. [65] gained the partial electron yield curve by monitoring 384-eV Auger electrons from N2, revealing similar double-excitation structures as observed in the angle-resolved ion detection measurement, but with a smaller background [67]. However, the poor resolution in their study hindered the clear identification of the doubly excited states. Although it was considered that the 384-eV electrons were due to atomic Auger decay following ultrafast dissociation, Naves de Brito et al. [68] concluded later that the corresponding electrons are associated with the formation of the C and 22Πg states of N.

The multielectron processes due to the electron correlation, such as the shake-up and shake-off transitions, are known to happen not only in the primary inner-shell hole creation processes, but also in their relaxation processes. In the case of the shake-off transition, where two electrons are ejected simultaneously, the great intensity of the peaks in the zero-kinetic-energy (ZEKE) electron spectrum arises through energy sharing between the two emitted electrons as their kinetic energy distribution is peaked with one electron having a low kinetic energy electron and the other having a correspondingly high kinetic energy. Thus, the ZEKE spectroscopy is very sensitive to this two-electron process. Additional information on the multiply excited states in the core-ionization continua can be gained by the combination of ARPIS with ZEKE, which can be called “symmetry-resolved zero-kinetic-energy (SR–ZEKE) photoelectron spectroscopy. This spectroscopy is realized by the coincident detection between the ZEKE photoelectrons and angle-resolved fragment ions. Although the symmetries of the multiply excited states and the photoelectron satellites in the K-shell ionization regions of CO [172] and N2 [173] was investigated under a high-resolution condition, clear symmetry identifications for the multielectron processes in the continuum were not given owing to the poor statistics of the SR–ZEKE spectra obtained.

Here, it is demonstrated that angle-resolved detection of metastable fragments is an effective spectroscopic tool for probing multiply excited states in molecules. It has already been shown that the production of metastable fragments N* is favored after the decay of the core-excited N2 states lying below the 1s ionization threshold [174]. The N* fragments are produced through the resonant Auger decay of the core-excited states into N states that subsequently undergo dissociation into N++N* [174]. The angle-resolved metastable yield curves above the 1s threshold exhibit multiexcitation structures with symmetry information. It is presented that the observation of metastable fragments enables the identification of multiexcitation structures with no significant background contribution from the ionization continuum [175].

The experimental setup for metastable detection is essentially the same as indicated in Fig. 1, but the applying voltages to the grids and MCP are different. The retarding grids were held at +80 V and the front plates of the two microchannel plate stacks at −2 kV. This arrangement prevents the detection of charged particles, ensuring that the detectors are sensitive only to neutral metastable particles with sufficient internal energy (>9 eV) and fluorescence photons in the vacuum ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray ranges. The geometry of the setup ensures that only (energetic) fragment N* metastables are detected, since the parent molecules maintain the velocity distribution inherent to the effusive beam. Figure 20 denotes the metastable yield curves recorded in the photon energy region of 405.7–430 eV in N2 at 0 and 90 with respect to the electric vector. The photon energy resolution was set to 200 meV. Below the 1s threshold, peaks due to Rydberg excitations are observed. Resonant Auger decay of the Rydberg states into N states and the subsequent dissociation into N++N* result in the N* formation [174]. Rydberg excitations associated with parallel transitions are observed in metastable yield at 0, and perpendicular transitions at 90, similar to the ion-yield curves of Fig. 5. This result implies that the emission directions of the metastable fragments essentially reflect the initial molecular orientations at the moment of photoexcitation, and that metastable observation enables us to resolve the symmetries of the Rydberg states. This conservation of molecular alignment indicates that the N dissociation following the Rydberg excitations is faster than the molecular rotation. Note that the finite acceptance angles of the detectors mix small amounts of parallel and perpendicular transition components into the 90 and 0 curves, respectively. In addition, a slight reduction of the initial orientations due to molecular rotation and/or an incomplete discrimination against fluorescence emissions with long lifetimes may be involved in the obtained spectra.

Figure 20. Angle-resolved metastable yield curves of N2 measured at 0 and 90 with respect to the electric vector. The photon energy resolution was set to 200 meV.

Figure 21. Net O− yield curve obtained in the O 1s excitation region of CO2, and O− images measured at the three photon energies indicated. The photon bandwidth was set to 0.16 eV, except for the image observations at hν=548.9 and 553.5 eV, where the bandwidth was set to 0.5 eV.

Higher Rydberg states produce metastable fragments more efficiently [174, 176], resulting in the large peaks around the 1s threshold on the metastable yield curves. The same N states formed by resonant Auger decay from the high Rydberg states also can be produced by the recapture of slow photoelectrons due to postcollision interaction [176]; the tails at the high-energy sides of the large peaks reflect the recapture probability [174]. The metastable yields decrease above the 1s ionization threshold, in contrast to the ionization continuum behaviors of the ion yields. This is because inner-shell photoionization rarely results in the formation of N*, and therefore the 1s ionization continuum hardly affects the metastable observation. In contrast, multiply excited states can produce N* if the states undergo resonant Auger decay into N states dissociating to N++N*. Many structures above the ionization threshold are observed in Fig. 20, and are attributable to multiply excited states.

Hikosaka et al. [175] also measured the metastable yield curves in the doubly excitation region (412.5–417.5 eV) with a narrower photon bandwidth (40 meV) and better statistics. The benefit of metastable observation is more pronounced for the Σ-symmetry states: the 0 curve clearly reveals the double-excitation structures that are seen as a shoulder (label E) on the shape resonance enhancement of the 0 ion yield curve in Fig. 5. A configuration-interaction calculation locates in this energy range one Σ-symmetry state with the electronic configuration of and two Π-symmetry states with as discussed in Section III. These states should appear as broad peaks reflecting photoexcitation to the repulsive walls of the potential energy curves. Narrow peaks are superimposed on broad structures. The single vibrational progression starting at 414.01 eV [17] is ascribable to the Rydberg-type doubly excited state . Through the data analysis, it is found that two new vibrational progressions, one Σ and one Π state, are discernible at 416–417 eV on the metastable yield curves [175]. It is nicely demonstrated that the observation of metastable fragments enables us to identify multiexcitation structures almost free from background contributions from the ionization continuum.

C. Negative Ion Detection

The observation of negative fragment ions can also be a sensitive probe of the multiply excited states embedded in the inner-shell ionization continuum, in the case where the molecules decay through the emission of stable negative fragment ions [177]. Formation of negative fragment ion has been explored in the inner-shell regions of simple molecules, since the first observation in the S 2p region of SO2 [178]. The investigations have revealed that negative ion formation is enhanced at core-excited states and not associated with inner-shell ionization. While it had been presumed that negative ion is emitted from singly charged ion states produced by resonant Auger decay of core-excited states, the direct evidence to the mechanism was recently offered by a negative–positive ion coincidence measurement [179]. Lindle and co-workers proved that the observation of negative fragment ions can be a probe to postcollision interaction [180] and to doubly excited states embedded in inner-shell ionization continua [181].

Traditionally, measurements of negative ion yields have been performed with mass spectrometric methods. Ordinary mass spectrometry, however, rarely possesses the ability to determine kinetic energies and angular distributions of negative ions, although the information derived from these species is useful for determining the electronic characters of the relevant core-excited states. It is also interesting to study the dynamical property on the negative ion productions. Recently, Hikosaka et al. [177] introduced the imaging technique into the observation of the negative ions in the molecular inner-shell region, in order to gain information on the kinetic energies and angular distributions of the particles concerned. As an example, the imaging observation on the negative ion formations in the vicinity of the O 1s ionization thresholds of CO2 is demonstrated here.

In a previous work [182], not only O− fragments, but also C− fragments, have been observed in the O 1s photoexcitation region of CO2, where the relative intensity was not noted. However, only O− formation is discernible on the time spectra measured at several photon energies in the O 1s region; Hikosaka et al. [177] concluded that C− formation is much weaker than O− formation. A net O− yield curve in the O 1s region is shown in Fig. 21, together with the O− images measured at three photon energies. The spectral features observed agree with those in the previously obtained spectrum [182]. The π* and Rydberg resonances below the O 1s ionization threshold are essentially the same as those interpreted well by photoabsorption and ion-yield measurements [183, 184]. The O− image observed at the π* resonance shows O− emissions preferably into the direction perpendicular to the electric vector, as expected from the symmetry consideration. The kinetic energy distribution deduced from the image is similar to that at the C 1s → π* resonance. The broad structures above the ionization threshold are allocated to doubly excited states, while the photoabsorption and photoionization spectra indicate only the structure around hν=547 eV [185, 186]. Weak preferences in the O− emissions perpendicular to the electric vector can be seen on both the images, suggesting superior perpendicular transitions at these photon energies.

Chapter 3

Geometric optimal control of simple quantum systems

Dominique Sugny

Laboratorie Interdisciplinaire Carnot de Bourgogne (ICB), UMR 5209 CNRS-Université de BourgogneF-21078 Dijon Cedex, France

I. Introduction

Optimal control theory can be viewed as a generalization of the classical calculus of variations for problems with dynamical constraints. Optimal control theory was born in its modern version with the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) in the late 1950s [1]. Its development was originally inspired by problems of space dynamics, but it is now a key tool to study a large spectrum of applications, such as robotics, economics, and quantum mechanics. Solving an optimal control problem means finding a particular control law (i.e., a particular pulse sequence), the optimal control, such that the corresponding trajectory satisfies given boundary conditions and minimizes a cost criterion. The cost functionals of physical interests are the energy of the field and the duration of the control. The strategy for solving an optimal control problem consists in finding extremal trajectories that are solutions of a generalized Hamiltonian system subject to the maximization condition of the PMP. In a second step, one selects among the extremals, the ones that effectively minimize the cost criterion. Although its implementation looks straightforward, the practical use of the PMP is far from being trivial and each control has to be analyzed using geometric and numerical methods. The first applications of optimal control theory in the control of quantum dynamics began in the mid-1980's. Continuous advances have been made both theoretically and experimentally [2–4]. The optimal equations can be solved by purely numerical techniques, such as the gradient algorithm, the monotonically convergent algorithms [5–7], or by using geometric tools [1, 8–12]. Due to the complexity of realistic systems with multiple degrees of freedom, the numerical approach 129 seems to be the only possible way to achieve control. More geometric aspects of the control can be formulated only for the simplest quantum systems having few levels (typically two or three) or consisting of coupled spin 1/2 particles [13]. The description of the geometric aspects of the control problems has not been widely used in the chemical physics literature and only few results exist in quantum mechanics mainly for closed quantum systems (see [14–19] to cite a few). The aim of this chapter is to present some of the tools of geometric optimal control theory that can be used in quantum control. For that purpose, we consider some simple examples as the control by laser fields of three-level conservative systems and of two-level dissipative systems. In a first approach, we skip most of the mathematical details. The reader is referred to standard mathematical textbooks for a complete and rigorous development of geometric optimal control theory [1, 8–10, 20]. Finally, we point out that the controllability analysis that is the first part of the study of an optimal control problem will not be discussed in this chapter (see, e.g., [21–26]). The controllability problem consists in determining if there exists a path going from the initial to the target state. This property will be assumed throughout this chapter.

This chapter is organized as follows: In Section II, we introduce the PMP and we state the theorem in the different cases that can be encountered in practice. The techniques associated to the use of the PMP, that is, indirect and continuation methods or the second-order optimality conditions are also detailed. Such tools allow us to compute the extremal solutions of the PMP and to determine their local optimality. Sections III and IV are devoted to the application of the PMP to the control of quantum systems. Section III deals with the optimal control of a three-level quantum system by laser fields plus von Neumann measurements. This three-level system corresponds to the Grushin model on the sphere that is one of the basic models in geometric optimal control. In particular, global optimality results can be obtained for this model. In Section IV, we solve the problem of the time-minimum control of two-level dissipative quantum systems by one or two control fields. For this example, we use the continuation techniques and the second-order optimality conditions. A realistic example in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) of the control of a spin 1/2 particle in a dissipative environment is also treated. Conclusion and prospective views are given in Section V.

Geometric Interpretation

An equivalent statement of the fact that the image of the map E' is is the following. A regular control means that, by varying u by a small amount δu, one can reach any point in a neighborhood of the final point x(T, x0, u). This notion can be more precisely defined as follows. We introduce the set A of accessible states in time T from x0:

Let x1 = x(T) be a point reached in time T from x0 by a regular trajectory. Then the accessibility set A(x0, T) is a neighborhood of the point x1, which implies that the system is locally controllable around x1. If x(T)∂A(x0, T) (i.e., the boundary of A), then u is said to be singular on [0, T]. This case is schematically illustrated in Fig. 2 for a regular and singular control field. The most interesting case is therefore the singular one and this case can be viewed as a first step toward the maximum principle. Indeed, a key observation for this principle is that if the trajectory (x, u) is optimal, then the point x(T, x0, u) must belong to the boundary of the accessibility set. This assertion can be understood in the time-minimal case, where the goal is to reach the target state x1 in minimum time. It is clear that if x1 = x(x0, T, u) belongs to the interior of A(x0, T), then one can find a smaller time T'<T and a point x(x0, T', u') of ∂A(x0, T), such that x1 = x(x0, T', u') (one can draw the accessibility set at different times to be convinced of this point). This result finally implies that u is not optimal for this control problem.

Figure 2. Schematic representation of the accessibility set A(x0, T) in gray. The control fields u1 and u2 are respectively singular, and regular.

C. Geometric Aspects of the Optimal Control Theory

This chapter gives a heuristic introduction to the geometric tools of optimal control theory.

The goal of geometric optimal control theory is to analyze the trajectories of the Hamiltonian system given by the PMP from a geometric point of view in order to deduce the geometric properties of the extremals: smooth or broken, number of switchings (a switching time is a time where the control field is discontinuous). An important point of this analysis is the fact that the PMP is only a necessary condition of optimality and one difficulty of the problem is to determine the cut point, that is, the first point along a given trajectory where the extremal ceases to be optimal. The computation of the cut point is a very difficult problem since it is a global problem, where all the Hamiltonian trajectories starting from the same initial point can play a role. In particular cases, one can determine geometrically the cut points that correspond to the points where two extremals with the same cost intersect. Figure 6 displays this situation (see below for a more concrete example). The optimal control problem consists in minimizing the length of the trajectory going from A to the final point. In Fig. 6, we consider two different optimal trajectories starting from point A. We can show that the red extremal is not optimal to go from A to D since in the BCD triangle, the BD length is smaller than the sum of the lengths BC and CD.

Figure 6. Broken solution to go from A to D with the shortest length. The extremals in red and blue starting from the point A intersect in C with the same length. The red extremal is not optimal from the point C since one can construct a broken solution ABD with a shortest length. (See insert for color representation of the figure.)

The computation of the cut points is global, but it is related to the computation of conjugate points. A conjugate point is a point where the extremal loses its local optimality when considering only extremals in a neighborhood of the first extremal (see Fig. 9 for an illustration). From a physical point of view, a conjugate point corresponds to a point where the extremals starting from the same initial point concentrate in a neighborhood of the conjugate point. This concept is analogous to the concept of caustic in optics. A numerical algorithm detailed in Section II. E can be used to determine the position of the conjugate points. For a fixed initial condition, the set of cut and conjugate points are, respectively, called the cut and the conjugate loci.

The problems of quantum control that we consider in this chapter are related to the Grushin model on the sphere. This model is a Riemannian model defined by the metric g = dϕ2+tan2ϕdθ2, where ϕ is the polar angle and θ the azimuthal angle of the spherical coordinates. Let x0 and x1 be two points on the sphere and γ a smooth path going from x0 to x1. We assume that γ can be parameterized by two functions tϕ(t) and tθ(t), where t[0, T]. The length L of the path given by the Grushin metric is equal to

Note that this length does not depend on the parameterization. Parameterizing this path by arclength, we minimize the time to go from x0 to x1 [14]. To parameterize a curve by arclength means that a new time τ, associated to the length of the curve, is defined as follows:

and the cost is equal to , where τf is the control duration.

The metric g allows us to determine the length between two points on the sphere. Then, it defines an optimization problem if we look for the shortest path going from one point to the other.

One can also use another metric that is the restriction of the euclidian metric to the sphere. The metric can be written as:

The cut and the conjugate loci can be determined for these two metrics. The results are represented in Figs. 7 and 8. For the euclidian metric, the shortest path to join two points is an arc of a big circle. The first conjugate point that corresponds in this case to the cut point is reached when the length of the arc is equal to π and this point is the antipodal point of the initial point. This situation is not generic for the metrics on the sphere and it is related to the symmetries of the problem. The situation is more generic for the Grushin metric. In this case, the cut locus is a subset of the antipodal parallel of the initial point, as illustrated in Fig. 8. The cut locus is not reduced to a point, except if the initial point is a pole. The conjugate and cut loci of a pole is the antipodal point for the Grushin metric. Note that this metric also has a singularity on the equator. The conjugate locus is plotted in blue in Fig. 8. This locus has an astroid shape. Different extremals have been represented. D. Indirect and Continuation Methods

In this section, we present some numerical methods to solve an optimal control problem.

We consider a problem with a given initial state x(0) and a target state x(T), where the control duration T can be fixed or not. Two types of numerical methods can be distinguished in optimal control to solve this problem, namely, the direct and the indirect methods. The direct approach consists in discretizing both the state of the system and the control, which reduces the optimal control problem to a nonlinear optimization problem (nonlinear programming). The indirect approach consists in solving, by a shooting method, a boundary problem given by the application of the PMP [28]. More precisely, this means that in the regular case one has to determine the initial adjoint state p(0) such that the corresponding Hamiltonian trajectory with initial conditions [x(0), p(0)] goes to x(T) at time T. This question can be very difficult to answer, in particular, if the dimension of the phase space is large. Another difficulty, which is not described here, is to take into account the singular extremals. The main drawback of indirect methods is their small domain of convergence with respect to the one of direct methods. They are, however, more accurate than the direct ones, which explains why there exist also hybrid approaches combining the advantages of the two methods. A geometric analysis of the optimal control problem can also be done in order to reduce the dimensionality of the problem, which simplifies the use of a shooting method. To summarize, if one has a sufficiently good approximation of p(0), one can use an indirect method and, for example, a standard Newton-type algorithm to solve the optimal control problem.

Another possibility is to use a continuation method. A smooth continuation method consists in the following. Suppose one wants to find a solution of a system of equations

where F is a smooth mapping. We consider a smooth homotopy path H(x, λ), such that H(x, 0)=G(x) and H(x, 1)=F(x), where G is a map having known zero points. In a smooth numerical continuation method (see [29]), the solutions are computed iteratively along this path using, for example, a Newton-type algorithm, the trial solutions at one step being given by the solutions of the previous step. This general method can be applied in Optimal Control. Indeed, as mentioned above, the optimal solution for a fixed set of boundary conditions can be computed by solving a shooting equation and the smooth continuation method can be applied if one can construct a smooth homotopy path between different optimal control problems. Different continuation methods exist in the literature, such as the discrete one which uses a Newton-type algorithm at each step, or the smooth one that uses the derivatives of the Hamiltonian trajectories along the homotopy path. An example will be given in Section IV for the optimal control of two-level dissipative quantum systems, where we illustrate the practical implementation of this algorithm.

E. Second-Order Optimality Conditions: The Concept of Conjugate Points

The second-order optimality conditions are used to determine the local optimality of extremal trajectories. By using the PMP for an open set U of values of the control fields, an optimal control has to satisfy the conditions ∂H/∂u = 0 and ∂2H/∂u2≤0, where H(x, p, u) is the pseudo-Hamiltonian. The condition on the second derivative corresponds to the local optimality of the control, that is, when one considers the extremals in a neighborhood of the reference trajectory (see Fig. 9 for an illustration). Now, we assume that ∂2H/∂u2<0 along a given extremal z=(x, p). A conjugate point will be the first point of the trajectory for which this relation does not hold. A conjugate point is therefore the point where the trajectory ceases to be optimal. Some tools have to be introduced to compute the position of this conjugate point.

which is called the Jacobi equation. Explicitly, this means that δz=(δx, δp) is solution of the system

with δx(0) = 0 and δp(0)=p0. A Jacobi field is a nontrivial solution of this equation. It is said to be vertical at time t if δx(t) = 0.

Next, we fix x0 = x(0) and introduce the exponential mapping

Let L0 be the space of points of the form {x0, p}. The tangent space of L0 is spanned by the n vertical Jacobi fields at time t = 0, since this space is locally diffeomorphic to . If the final time is not fixed, the PMP yields the additional condition H = 0 and the dimension of this space is at most n−1 (see below for a concrete computation of the basis of this tangent space). We then introduce the space Lt that is the image of L0 at time t by the map . The tangent space at time t of Lt is spanned by the Jacobi fields image by the linearized system (8) of the initial vertical Jacobi fields. A time tc is said to be conjugate if there exists a Jacobi field that is vertical at time tc. This is a precise formulation of the physical intuition of accumulation of trajectories at a conjugate point since for a vertical Jacobi field one has δx(tc) = 0. This behavior is analogous to the concept of caustics in optics. Under suitable assumptions, it can then be shown that the trajectory is locally optimal up to the first conjugate point [30]. A schematic description of the evolution of the set Lt is represented in Fig. 10. Using this idea, different numerical algorithms can be used to determine the position of conjugate points.

A second test is to compute the n Jacobi fields Ji(t)=(δxi(t), δpi(t)), i = 1, . . ., n such that δpi(0)=ei, i = 1, . . ., n. In this case, the rank condition reads

Using these different tests, the numerical implementation of the computation of conjugate points is relatively straightforward. One has to integrate differential equations and to compute the rank or the determinant of a matrix. The singular value decomposition of this matrix is an efficient way to determine the variation of the rank of a matrix. The rank decreases by one when one of the singular values vanishes. Some examples will be given in Section IV for the time-optimal control of two-level dissipative quantum systems.

The different tests are implemented in the COTCOT software (Conditions of Order Two and COnjugates Times [30]) that can be downloaded free from the website of [31].

The interaction of the system with the laser field consists of a dipolar interaction with constant dipolar terms coupling only neighboring states. It is known that this type of system is not completely controllable by unitary evolution [32]. The noncomplete controllability of the system can be understood geometrically as follows: We define new coordinates Xi by

The radii Ri and Rf of the two spheres are determined from the initial state of the system and are constant for unitary evolution. To simplify the geometrical description of the control, we consider in this chapter that one of the radius is equal to one and the other to zero. In this case, we can assume that the state belongs only to one sphere since the dynamics on the other sphere is trivial. Using this description, one deduces that if the system is initially on one of the two spheres, then it will remain on this sphere by unitary evolution and it will not reach a state belonging, for example, to the other sphere. The description of the control is more difficult if the two radii are different from zero. In particular, due to the symmetry of Eq. (15), the optimal trajectories on the two spheres are the same and cannot be controlled independently.

C. Optimal Control of a Three-Level Quantum System by Laser Fields and von Neumann Measurements

Now, we describe the control assisted by von Neumann measurements (VNMs). The VNMs can be classified into two types: the instantaneous measurements and the continuous ones. Among instantaneous measurements, we also distinguish the selective ones where the state after the measurement is known (with a given probability) and the nonselective ones where this state is unknown [36]. Here, we will only consider selective instantaneous measurements. The question of the measurement driven quantum evolution has already been discussed in a series of work mainly from a numerical point of view (see [36-40] to cite a few), either with or without a laser field assisting the control. In this section, we revisit this problem by using the PMP and a more geometrical point of view.

We assume that the initial and the target states belong, respectively, to the two spheres Si and Sf. We can choose, for example, |ψi=|2 and . For the measurement process, the idea is to determine an observable Q for which the system passes from Si to Sf after a measurement. We thus see that the introduction of measurements allows us to create a path from the initial state to the target state. This is possible if all the eigenvectors of Q belong to Sf and form a basis of . A possible choice is given by the vectors

The corresponding observable Q is equal to , where the qi's are real numbers. Let be the state of the system at time t. Then after the measurement, this state becomes |ϕi (i{1, 2, 3}) with the probability |ai|2. Since all the eigenvectors of Q belong to Sf, the sphere of the target state, one sees that, whatever the result of the measurement, the target state can now be reached by unitary evolution. Note also that the control by laser field on the sphere Sf will depend on the result of the measurement. We assume that the operator knows this result and can modify the control field according to the result of the measurement.

To solve this problem, we begin by the standard formulation of the PMP, (i.e., without measurement), as shown in Section III. B. Then, we assume that a measurement is performed at a time t[0, T]. The definition of the cost given below can be extended straightforwardly to the case of several measurements. We denote by |ψ(t) the state of the system at time t at which the measurement is performed. Since {ϕi}(i = 1,,3) is a basis of , |ψ(t) can be written as:

Let C0(t) be the cost corresponding to the optimal path from |ψi to |ψ(t). Note that C0 is equal to zero if t = 0. We also introduce the costs Ci, (i = 1, . . ., 3) which are, respectively, associated to the optimal passage from |ϕi to |ψf. The total cost of the control C(t) is then defined by

The choice of C(t) is related to the fact that the operator knows the result of the measurement and can modify the electric field accordingly. Here, can be viewed as an average of the three costs Ci. From the cost C(t), the goal is then to determine the control fields, the observable Q and the time t at which the measurement is performed to minimize C(t). We will solve this problem by using twice the PMP: Once on Si and once on Sf. Indeed, for a fixed observable Q, it is clear that the trajectories that minimize C correspond to the concatenation of extremal trajectories on Si and Sf. We solve this optimal control problem in Section IV for particular examples. The general solution is very complex and can only be determined numerically.

IV. Application to the Time-Optimal Control of Two-Level Dissipative Quantum Systems

The objective of this section is to describe the geometric aspects of the optimal control of two-level dissipative quantum systems. When a quantum system interacts with a Markovian or a non-markovian bath, the control field cannot generally fully compensate the dissipation effect that largely enhances the difficulty of the control. This point has been rigourously shown in [21] for a dynamics governed by the Lindblad equation [41-43]. In this context, several studies using numerical optimization techniques have proved that efficient control can still be achieved (see [44-50] to cite a few). We propose here to give a geometric analysis of this question in the time-minimal case, the maximum of the control field being fixed to an arbitrary value. Note that this cost functional is particularly relevant in the context of a dissipative environment especially when the dissipation effect is undesirable to reach the target state.

A. The Kossakowski–Lindblad Equation for N-Level Dissipative Quantum Systems

First, we recall the form of the Kossakowski–Lindblad equation for an N-level quantum system described by a density operator ρ[41-52]. The dynamics of ρ is governed by the following first-order differential equation:

(34)

This equation differs from the standard von Neumann equation in that a dissipation operator LD acting on the set of density operators has been added. This linear operator, describes the interaction with the environment, cannot be chosen arbitrarily. Under particular assumptions, such as the semigroup dynamics, the norm continuity, and the conservation of probability [41, 42], the form of LD can be deduced from a rigorous mathematical analysis. In this form, the coefficient akk' has to be positive to ensure the complete positivity of the density matrix. A particular choice for the matrices Vk is the following. The parameter L2 describes the reverse process, that is, the passage |1 to |2 with absorption of energy. Here, L3 represents pure dephasing processes [51].

3. The Optimal Control Problem

In this section, we analyze the singularities of the Hamiltonian system in order to deduce the properties of the optimal trajectories. We obtain that every optimal trajectory can be of two types.

  • In the first case, the trajectory is external with pθ = 0, contained in a meridian plane, which is a time-optimal solution of the 2D system, where x=(0, y, z) and u=(u1, 0).
  • In the second case, the trajectory is the connection of smooth extremal arcs, which are solutions of the Hamiltonian H with pθ≠0, while the only possible connections are located in the equatorial plane ϕ = π/2.

Some work has to be done to obtain a regularity result about optimal trajectories. This is due to the existence of a switching surface Σ:P1 = P2 = 0 in which we can connect two extremal arcs, provided we respect the Erdmann–Weierstrass conditions at the junction, that is, the adjoint vector remains continuous and the Hamiltonian is constant [53, 54]. The set Σ can also contain singular arcs for which P1 = P2 = 0 holds identically. Hence, we can have intricate behaviors for such systems. In our case, the situation is simplified by the symmetry of revolution. Indeed, if pθ = 0 then the singularities are related to the classification of extremals in the single-control case. We cannot connect an extremal with pθ≠0 to an extremal, where pθ = 0, since the adjoint vector has to be continuous. Hence, the only remaining possibility is to connect two extremals with pθ≠0 at a point of Σ leading to the conditions pϕ = 0 and pθcotϕ = 0 in spherical coordinates. Since pθ≠0, one gets ϕ = π/2. The result is proved.

From this preliminary analysis, we observe that the time-minimal control problem can be analyzed in two steps. For physical reasons, the initial condition is taken as a pure state that is on the Bloch sphere.

  • Initial condition on the (Oz)-axis: In this case, using the symmetry group, the extremal synthesis is equivalent up to a rotation around (Oz) to the one of a planar system on x = 0 with u2 = 0 and |u1|≤1. We use standard techniques [9] and the main features of the syntheses are described in Section IV.D.
  • Initial condition not on the (Oz)-axis: We start the analysis from the case Γ=γ+ and γ− = 0, which is a singular case where the purity r of the system is not controllable and the time minimal analysis corresponds precisely to the Grushin case on the two sphere. Then, we deform this system in order to deduce the properties of the model in the general case. We show in particular that the Hamiltonian system is integrable for γ− = 0, which allows us to analytically solve the optimal control problem. In the case, γ−≠0, we use a numerical analysis to conclude.

For γ− = 0, this set is reduced to the origin (y = 0, z = 0). The set C has the following physical interpretation. The purity of a quantum state is here defined by the function 2Tr[ρ2]−1=y2+z2. The set C divides the plane (y, z) into a region where the purity of the state locally increases and a region where it locally decreases. On the boundary, the purity is preserved. This point can be understood as follows. The conservative vector field G is orthoradial for each point (y, z)≠(0, 0) of the manifold. The vector field F does not modify the purity of the state if the radial component of F vanishes, that is, if F is parallel to G, which is the definition of C. Next, we analyze the fixed points of the dynamics when the field is on, which are defined by F+uG = 0. Since F and G are parallel, the fixed points belong to C. Inversely, one can ask if every point of C corresponds to a limit point of the dynamics. The answer is positive for a real nonbounded control u since the limits can be written

As suggested by its name, the clock form is a form that allows one to determine the time taken to travel a path and to compare the extremals. Let γ be a path in the plane (y, z), which does not cross C and T the time of travel along γ. We have

Turnpike and Antiturnpike Curves

Not every trajectory lying in the set S can be an optimal trajectory. In order to characterize this point, we introduce the notion of turnpike and antiturnpike curves [9]. Let x∉S∪C and the function f(x)=−ΔS(x)/ΔC(x). A turnpike curve is an arc lying in S∪Cc such that for every point x of this arc X(x) and Y(x) are not tangent to S. It is also assumed that X(x) and Y(x) point to opposite sides of S that define two regions Ωx and Ωy. If f(x)>0 (resp. f(x)<0) on Ωy and f(x)<0 (respectively f(x)>0) on Ωx then the arc is a turnpike (resp. antiturnpike) arc. The relation with the optimal synthesis can be stated as follows: Using the clock form α, it can be shown that the antiturnpike trajectories are not optimal. Figure 17 displays the turnpike and the antiturnpike curves for particular values of the dissipative parameters.

3. Four Different Illustrative Examples

We consider four different qualitative cases of control that allow us to study several physically relevant situations. A pure state is characterized by y2+z2 = 1 and a mixed state by y2+z2≤1.

  • Case (a): Conversion of a pure state into a mixed state with (γ−/γ+ = 0, Γ>γ++2).
  • Case (b): Conversion of a pure state into a mixed state with (γ−/γ+ = 0, γ+−2<Γ<γ++2).
  • Case (c): Purification of the completely random mixed state that corresponds to the center of the Bloch ball (γ−/γ+=−1, Γ>γ++2).
  • Case (d): Conversion of a pure state into a mixed state with (γ−/γ+=−0.5, Γ>γ++2).

To answer this question, we use the switching function Φ. For x(t)CS∪S, Φ(t) = 0, that is, the vectors p(t) and G(x(t)) are orthogonal. Since the direction of G is known (G is orthoradial), one can deduce the direction of p(t). Let z1 and z2 be two points belonging, respectively, to CS and S. The vectors G(z) associated to these points are schematically represented in Fig. 23. Now, we let the states z1 and z2 go to (0, 0) and we determine the directions of the different adjoint states. We recall that the PMP states that p is a continuous function that does not vanish. When z1 goes to (0, 0), one deduces by a continuity argument that p1 is vertical in O. When z2 goes to (0, 0), the limit direction of p2 is given by the switch curve CS. To respect the continuity of p, one sees that CS has to be tangent to the line y = 0 in O. Due to the complexity of analytical calculations, we have checked numerically that this is not the case. The singular line for z<0 is therefore not optimal.

Physical Interpretation

From the results obtained in the preceding paragraphs, some qualitative conclusions can be made with respect to the dissipation effect on the time optimal control of the dynamics. The dissipation is not undesirable when the dissipation allows us to purify the system [cases (c) and (d)] and help accelerating the control. In contrast, for the conversion of a pure state into a mixed state, the dissipation alone increases the duration of the control and its effect is not beneficial for the control [cases (a) and (b)]. Example (d) summarizes the situation well. As long as the purity of the state decreases, it is advantageous to use a control field, but when the purity starts increasing the dissipation alone becomes more efficient.

E. Application to the Optimal Control in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance

One of the most promising fields of applications of geometric optimal control in quantum control is the control of spin systems in NMR [13, 56]. Here, we apply the previous computations to a physical example, namely, the optimal control by a magnetic field of a spin 1/2 particle in interaction with an environment [13, 17]. To simplify the discussion, we assume that the frequency of the control field is resonant with the transition frequency of the spin [15]. Taking uy = 0, we are thus considering a single-input problem in a plane of the form:

One deduces that the singular control vanishes on the vertical singular line and that it is admissible, that is, |us|≤2π, on the horizontal one if |y|≥|γ(γ−2Γ)|/[2π(2Γ−2γ)]. For smaller values of y, the system cannot follow the horizontal singular arc and a switching curve appears from the point where the admissibility is lost [9]. The optimality of the singular trajectories can be determined geometrically by using the clock form. It can be shown that the horizontal singular line is locally optimal and that the vertical one is optimal if z>z0.

We consider the control problems defined by the relaxation parameters γ−1 and Γ−1 (expressed in the normalized time unit defined above) of 23.9 and 1.94, respectively, and M0≈2.15×10−5. We compare the optimal control law with an intuitive one used in NMR. The intuitive solution is composed of a bang pulse to reach the opposite point of the initial state along the z-axis followed by a zero control, where we let the dissipation act up to the center of the Bloch ball. The optimal and the intuitive solutions are plotted in Fig. 24. Geometric tools allow us to show that the optimal control is the concatenation of a bang pulse, followed successively by a singular control along the horizontal singular line, another bang pulse and a zero singular control along the vertical singular line. Figure 24 also displays the switching curve that has been determined numerically by considering a series of trajectories with u=+2π originating from the horizontal singular set, where ϕ = 0. The points of the switching curve correspond to the first point of each trajectory where the switching function vanishes. To determine the optimal control law, we have also checked that the second bang pulse of the optimal sequence does not cross the switching curve up to the vertical singular axis. In this example, a gain of 58% is obtained for the optimal solution over the intuitive one, which shows the interest of geometric techniques.

F. Time-Optimal Control of Two-Level Dissipative Quantum Systems: The Double-Input Case

In this section, we study the optimal synthesis for the double-input case, that is, for the general case where two control fields are considered. The discussion is splitted into two cases: The case γ− = 0, which is the situation, where the extremal flow is integrable and the generic case, if γ−≠0. A more mathematical presentation of this question can be found in [53, 54].

1. The Integrable Case

For γ− = 0, the Hamiltonian H reads

Proof Using the change of coordinates ρ=lnr, H can be written

The case |Γ−γ+|<2

Now, we give the main result of this section that is established for |γ+−Γ|<2.

Proposition 9 For pρ and pθ>0 fixed, there exist two trajectories starting from (r(0), ϕ(0), θ(0)), which intersect with the same cost at a point such that ϕ = π−ϕ(0).

Note that the symmetry of the flow of H with respect to the meridian is preserved. More precisely, if pθ→−pθ, then we have two extremals with the same length symmetric with respect to the meridian, so we can assume pθ>0 in proposition 9. Some lemmas are required before the proof of proposition 9.

To determine the position of the intersection, we now consider the two extremal curves starting from the same point (r(0), ϕ(0), θ(0) = 0) and such that , where is given by (49) with ϕ = ϕ(0). These two extremals correspond to the curves of the function ϕθ translated from each other by a given angle θ, which depends on the initial conditions. It is then straightforward to see that these two extremals intersect with the same length on the antipodal parallel π−ϕ(0). Using the fact that the evolution of the radial coordinate r depends only on ϕ and the symmetry ϕ→π−ϕ, one deduces that not only the projections, but also the extremal curves intersect with the same length that concludes the proof.

As a corollary of proposition 9, we have the following result about the cut locus in the case |γ+−Γ|<2.

Corollary 1 Two extremals with nonzero p θ intersecting with the same time cannot be optimal beyond the intersecting point.

Proof The proof is standard. Assuming optimality beyond the intersecting point, we can construct a broken minimizer that is an extremal with nonzero pθ.

The case |Γ−γ+|≥2

Extremal curves have a more complex behavior for |Γ−γ+|≥2. We proceed as before by fixing pθ, pρ, and H = h. The projections of the extremals on the sphere in the coordinates (ϕ, θ) are either aperiodic or periodic according to the values of pθ, pρ, and h. Some general characteristics of the extremals can be determined and are described by the following results.

Aperiodic extremals are extremals such that ϕ is not periodic. They have an asymptotic fixed point (rf, ϕf, θf) and pϕ→±∞, when t→+∞. The possible fixed points are described by the following proposition:

Proposition 10 The projection of the asymptotic fixed point of the extremal on the sphere in the coordinates (θ, ϕ) is located on one of the parallels ϕf = α, ϕf = π/2−α, ϕf = π/2+α, and ϕf = π−α, where α=arcsin[2/|Γ−γ+|]/2. If Γ>γ+ (respectively, Γ<γ+), then only the fixed points such that ϕf = α or ϕf = π−α (respectively, ϕf = π/2−α or ϕf = π/2+α) can be reached depending on the initial value ϕ(0).

Proof Proposition 10 can be shown by solving the following equation deduced from the system (42):

Then, we determine the sign of the expression 1−(γ+−Γ)2sin2(2ϕ)/4 as a function of ϕ and we deduce that the derivative dϕ/dθ has no zero in]α, π/2−α[∪]π/2+α, π−α[. For Γ−γ+>2, a direct inspection of dϕ/dθ also shows that dϕ/dθ<0 (respectively, dϕ/dθ>0) if ϕ]α, π/2−α[(respectively, ϕ]π/2+α, π−α[), which indicates the parallel that can be reached. The same analysis can be undertaken for Γ−γ+<2, which completes the proof.

Note that the aperiodic extremals have no conjugate point and are always optimal. Periodic extremals occur in a band near the equator. They have the same properties as the extremals for |Γ−γ+|<2. In particular, two extremals of the same length intersect on the antipodal parallel.

The characteristics of the extremals are summarized in Fig. 26. Two periodic trajectories intersecting with the same length on the antipodal parallel are displayed. Other extremals are aperiodic with fixed points located on the parallel ϕf=arcsin[2/|Γ−γ+|]/2 or ϕf = π−arcsin[2/|Γ−γ+|]/2.

Numerical Determination of the Conjugate Locus

The goal of this section is to determine numerically the conjugate locus for the two-input case. We restrict the discussion to the case |Γ−γ+|<2. Following the previous section, numerical computations are undertaken in spherical coordinates for fixed coordinates pθ and pρ. As already mentioned, the case Γ=γ+ can be associated to the Grushin model, the drift vector field F0 being purely radial. In this model, the conjugate locus is known and described in Section II.C. This result is recalled in Fig. 27, where we represent the projection of the conjugate and cut loci on the sphere of radius 1 in the coordinates (θ, ϕ). The radial dependence is trivial in this case and depends on the value of Γ=γ+. Here, the important point to note is the fact that the projection of the conjugate locus on the sphere is independent of pr(0) for this model.

Figure 27. Extremal trajectories for the Grushin model corresponding to Γ= γ+ = 2. Conjugate and cut loci are represented in dashed line.

The idea is then to start from this model and to deform it by modifying the parameters γ+ and Γ with the constraint |Γ−γ+|<2. A first comparison between the two models is given by Figs. 27 and 28, where we observe that the global structure of the extremals is nearly the same. The same conclusion is obtained from the analysis of the radial coordinate whose evolution is not represented here. Figure 29 displays the projection of the conjugate locus on the sphere in the coordinates (θ, ϕ) for a given value of pr(0). We have added the locus of the Grushin model for comparison. Note that this locus is only slightly modified with respect to the one of the Grushin model. However, the projection on the sphere of the conjugate locus depends on pr(0) for Γ≠γ+.

Geometric Interpretation of the Integrable Case

A geometric analysis allows us a complete understanding of the two types of extremal behaviors. Indeed assuming γ− = 0, the restriction of the system to the two-sphere is

We observe that it defines a Zermelo navigation problem [57] on the sphere where the current is

and the metric is the Grushin metric on the two sphere

The drift can be compensated by a feedback if |γ+−Γ|<2. The problem is symmetric with respect to the equator and we can restrict our analysis to the upper hemisphere. We observe that the amplitude of the current is maximum for ϕ = π/4, while it is minimum at the North pole and at the equator. More generally, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 11 For the system restricted to the sphere we have two cases:

1. If |γ+−Γ|<2, it defines a Zermelo navigation problem on the whole sphere minus the equator for the Grushin metric on the sphere.

2. If |γ+−Γ|>2, the current can be compensated in the north equator except in a band centered at ϕ = π/4, hence defining a Zermelo navigation problem near the equator and near the North pole.

To complete the analysis, it is sufficient to describe the following barrier phenomenon. Let ψ = π/2−ϕ and assume that . Starting at the equator for which ψ = 0, when ψ increases, we meet a barrier corresponding to the singularity of the vector field. For example, if γ+−Γ>0, then we have a barrier for 1=[−sin(2ϕ)(γ+−Γ)/2].

This result explains the two types of extremal behaviors observed in the numerical simulations.

  • If |γ+−Γ|<2, the extremal curves restricted to the two sphere are periodic curves, as in the Grushin case.
  • If |γ+−Γ|>2, we have two types of extremal curves: Near the equator, since the current can be compensated, we have periodic curves. But if the trajectory is entering in the band where the current cannot be compensated, the barrier phenomenon appears and we observe the asymptotic behaviors of the extremals.

2. The Generic Case γ−≠0

In this section, we use mainly numerical simulations to describe extremal curves in the case γ−≠0. We concentrate on the description of the generic cases observed in the numerical simulations. We present numerical results about the behavior of extremal solutions and conjugate point analysis.

Extremal Trajectories

We begin by analyzing the structure of extremal trajectories. The description is based on a direct integration of the system. We observe two different asymptotic behaviors corresponding to stationary points of the dynamics that are described by the following results.

Conjugate Points

The Cotcot code is used to evaluate the conjugate points [31]. This occurs only in case (b) and the numerical simulations show that the first conjugate points appear before an uniform number of oscillations of the ϕ variable. This phenomenon is represented on Fig. 34. Cutting the trajectory at the first conjugate point avoids such a behavior. Note that due to the symmetry of revolution, the global optimality is lost for θ≤π.

3. Singular Value Decomposition

To illustrate the determination of the position of the conjugate points, here we consider the singular value decomposition of the matrix formed by the two Jacobi fields. It is this matrix that is used to compute the conjugate points.

Let p(0) be the initial value of the adjoint vector. We consider the two Jacobi fields such that p(0)·δp(0) = 0. We use the singular-value decomposition of the matrix of the two Jacobi fields to compute the two singular values. The rank of the matrix (δx1, δx2) decreases by one when one of the singular values vanishes. To compute the singular values, we have used the function svd of the Matlab software. Figures 35 – 38 show the evolution of the angle ϕ and the corresponding values of the singular values for different dissipative parameters. The singular value 1 is equal to 0 for the first conjugate point.

4. Continuation Method

The continuation method was both implemented in a simple numerical framework using MatLab routines (discretization of the parameter interval that can be normalized to [0, 1], and at each step the Newton routine was used to compute the root) and by using a smooth approach. In this second case, a unique shooting is necessary to initialize the continuation method.

For geometric reasons, the continuation method is splitted into two parts.

  • Continuation method for the reduced problem: The final purity is not controlled and the transversality condition pρ(tf) = 0 at the final time tf is added in the shooting equation.
  • Continuation method for the full problem. In this case, we have to check that the final purity belongs to the accessible set for every value of the dissipation parameters.

We present two numerical examples illustrating these two situations. The smooth and the discrete continuation approaches have been implemented in each case. By (pρf = 0, ϕf, θf) and (ρf, ϕf, θf) we denote, respectively, the target states of the control in the first and second cases. In the first case, where the final purity is not fixed, we consider the homotopy method with respect to the parameter Γ and in the second case a continuation with respect to γ−. Knowing the starting point of the continuation method [pρ(0), pϕ(0), tf], we use the two continuation algorithms to determine new triplets (pρ(0), pϕ(0), tf) such that the system reaches the same target state when the dissipation parameters vary. The adjoint state pθ is kept fixed in the computation, while the value of the Hamiltonian, which remains positive, changes at each step. Figures. 39 and 40 represent the different results we have obtained. In each case, the control duration is chosen small enough to be before the first conjugate point. Note the smooth evolution of the three parameters pϕ(0), pρ(0), and tf when the continuation parameters vary. The results of the two methods are very close to each other. The step size of the discrete approach is, respectively, taken to be 0.05 and 0.01 in the first and second cases. With this step size, which is not representative of our control problem (larger step size can be chosen), the Newton algorithm does not encounter any problem to converge. The shooting equation is solved with an accuracy better than 10−12 in the two continuation methods.

The target state corresponds to ϕf = 0.845096, θf = 0.04015590, and pρf = 0. Three figures represent the evolution of the adjoint states pρ(0) and pϕ(0) and of the control duration tf as a function of Γ for the Newton-type continuation (dashed line) and the smooth-type one (solid line). In the second case, when we consider a final condition on the radial coordinate, some problems of accessibility have been encountered. As a preliminary study, we have therefore to check that the target state belongs to the accessibility set for every value of the dissipation parameters used in the continuation method. When this condition is satisfied, we have observed no problem of convergence for the continuation method. This condition is more difficult to fulfill for long control durations. Figure 41 illustrates the constraint due to the accessibility set in the second case. For given values of dissipation parameters and of pρ, we have determined the values of pϕ(0) and tf allowing us to reach the point of coordinates (ϕf, θf). We have then plotted the corresponding radial coordinate ρf as a function of pρ. Note that the diagram is symmetric with respect to the vertical axis pρ = 0 and has roughly the same form up to vertical translations for different values of the dissipation parameters. Figure 41 shows the values of the radial coordinate ρf that can be reached when ϕf and θf are fixed. Using such a diagram for different dissipation parameters, one can check that the point (ρf, ϕf, θf) belongs to the accessible set. Figures 42 and 43 represent the evolution of the continuation parameters as a function of the number of steps. The step size of the Newton algorithm has been chosen so that the number of steps of the two approaches are roughly the same. Note the nontrivial behavior of the continuation parameter in the second case.

V. Conclusion

We hope that these different examples of application of techniques of geometric optimal control theory to simple quantum systems will motivate a systematic investigation of the geometric aspects in quantum control. We have investigated the optimal control of a conservative three-level quantum system and the time-optimal control of two-level dissipative quantum systems. In this context, an open question is the generalization of the present examples to more complex quantum systems having, for example, four or five levels or corresponding to two or three spins in interaction [17]. Due to the complexity of such systems, the determination of the optimal control law will require a more extensive numerical analysis than the one presented in this chapter. The same tools as the continuation method or the second-order optimality conditions can be used in this case.
